query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding optimized amounts of Al, Cr, and Si to refractory high-entropy alloys improves their high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale that retards oxygen diffusion.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a W-based or Nb-based system) without the optimized levels of Al, Cr, and Si, which exhibits significant oxide scale spallation and mass gain during high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base RHEA with controlled additions of aluminum, chromium, and silicon.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at 1000–1100 °C for extended durations (e.g., 50 to 200 hours), where oxidation and scale formation processes are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous oxide scale primarily composed of alumina (Al2O3) and chromium oxides (e.g., Cr2O3) with possible contributions from silicon-derived oxides, which enhances scale adhesion and limits oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the introduced Al, Cr, and Si elements preferentially oxidize to form stable and slow-growing protective oxide layers. These layers reduce the oxygen diffusion rate into the substrate, thereby decreasing the overall oxidation rate as compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and improved oxide scale adhesion with reduced spallation relative to the untreated alloy under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy that develops a less continuous and more spall-prone oxide layer, resulting in higher mass gain and degradation under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the alloying additions are optimized; excessive additions may lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds that could adversely affect mechanical integrity. The improvement is anticipated under the specified temperature range and atmospheric conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While prior literature supports the beneficial effects of these alloying elements in similar systems, the exact quantitative improvement and the optimal concentrations in RHEAs remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one group of refractory high-entropy alloys alloyed with the optimized amounts of Al, Cr, and Si, and a control group with the base composition. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C in air for 200 hours. After testing, measure the mass gain per unit area and perform microstructural analysis of the oxide layer using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate scale continuity and adhesion.
measurements: Phase composition of the scale (e.g., presence of Al2O3, Cr2O3, SiO2)
Adhesion quality of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloyed specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower mass gain) and improved scale continuity/adhesion compared to the untreated control, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 []. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [,,,,]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [,,,]. Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
